title: Deja's Food Drive and the Class Pet Vote
goal: I can divide with long division, check with multiplication, explain what a remainder means, and compare two viewpoints using evidence from the text.

card.desc: You learn long division with Deja's 552 cans: Divide, Multiply, Subtract, Bring down, with 1-digit and 2-digit divisors and a multiples list. You write remainders, check every answer with multiplication (your Lesson 1 skill), and decide what a remainder means in a story. Then you read Malia's and Theo's pieces from The Class Pet Vote and compare, contrast and weigh their evidence (Pathways Week 7).

win: You split the cans fairly, checked every answer and weighed both viewpoints. Deja's food drive is ready to deliver!

slides.title: Deja's Food Drive and the Class Pet Vote
slides.text: Deja's class collected 552 cans for 24 food pantries. Every pantry needs a fair share. Today you learn long division to split big numbers. Then you read two classmates who see a class vote very differently, and you compare their viewpoints. First: 20 minutes of Lesson 1 review, because long division uses multiplication in every step.

notes.do: Before class: check his Lesson 1 Show What You Know score (Formspree). Set out base-ten blocks: 5 flats, 15 rods and 32 units (5 flats, 5 rods, 2 units to build 552, plus 10 extra rods and 30 extra units for trading). Also an index card, two highlighters (two colors), whiteboard and marker, pencil and paper. Math runs 9:30–10:05 (35 min); reading runs 10:05–10:30 (25 min).
notes.say: Two jobs today. First 35 minutes: long division, step by step, with remainders and a check. Last 25 minutes: two kids, one class vote, and how to compare what they think.
notes.ask: What do you remember about division with leftovers? What was 45 ÷ 6?
notes.listen: 7 R3 (6 × 7 = 42, 3 left). If he hesitates, that is fine: today builds that exact skill.

slides.title: The tens row: 36 × 47
slides.text: The 4 in 47 is 4 tens, so the second row is 36 × 40, not 36 × 4.

steps.text: Tens row. Say “forty.” Write the 0 first. Then 36 × 4 = 144 goes in front of it: 1,440.
Add. 252 + 1,440 = 1,692. Estimate: 40 × 50 = 2,000. Close, so it makes sense.

slides.tip: The tens row always ends in 0. If it doesn't, stop and fix it.

notes.do: Build 36 × 40 with base-ten blocks or the place-value chart first: 4 groups of 36 is 144, and 40 groups is ten times that.
notes.say: When you multiply by 40, you are making groups of ten. That is why the 0 comes first.
notes.ask: Why is 36 × 4 not the tens row?
notes.listen: Because the 4 is in the tens place: it means 40.

slides.title: The tens row
slides.text: Paper first, then type.

items.no: Write the 0 first, then 56 × 4.
Write the 0, then 47 × 3.

items.q: In 68 × 27, what is the tens row?
no: That is 68 × 2. The 2 is 2 tens, so the row needs a 0.
That is the ones row, 68 × 7.
One zero too many: 68 × 20 is about 1,400, not 14,000.

notes.do: He says “twenty,” “forty,” “thirty” out loud before each one.
notes.say: Say the tens digit as tens.
notes.ask: What would 56 × 40 be if you forgot the 0?
notes.listen: 224, which is far too small. The estimate (60 × 40 = 2,400) catches it.

slides.title: Line up every column, then add
slides.text: On graph paper, put one digit in each square. Then add the two rows one column at a time, right to left.

steps.text: Tens: 7 + 6 = 13. Write 3, regroup the 1 above the hundreds.
Hundreds: 4 + 3 + the regrouped 1 = 8. Thousands: 1. Answer: 1,836.

slides.tip: Write every regrouped 1 above its column so you can see it when you add.

notes.do: He does 68 × 27 on graph paper with you, one digit per square. This was one he missed (he wrote 1,786).
notes.say: When the columns drift, the adding goes wrong. The squares keep them straight.
notes.ask: Where did 1,786 come from?
notes.listen: Usually a lost regroup in the tens or hundreds. Have him find it.

slides.title: Count the zeros
slides.text: Round, multiply the front digits, then count the zeros.

items.why: 7 × 2 = 14, then two zeros: 1,400.
no: Only one zero. 70 × 20 has two zeros.
One zero too many. 70 × 20 has two zeros, not three.
That is 70 × 30.

items.why: 8 × 4 = 32, then two zeros: 3,200.
items.no: 8 × 4, then count the zeros.

items.q: Someone got 68 × 27 = 18,360. Estimate: 70 × 30 = 2,100. What do you say?
choices: Close enough
Too big: about 10 times too big
Too small
items.why: 2,100 vs 18,360 is about 10 times too big: there is an extra 0. The real answer is 1,836.
no: 18,360 is nowhere near 2,100. Something is wrong.
18,360 is bigger than 2,100, not smaller.

notes.do: He writes the estimate in a box BEFORE every problem from now on.
notes.say: An estimate is only useful if it is right. Count the zeros.
notes.ask: When would an estimate NOT catch a mistake?
notes.listen: When the answer is close but wrong (like 1,786 vs 1,836). Then you recheck each step.

slides.title: Be the checker
slides.text: Check each row yourself on paper before you choose.

items.q: Someone wrote: 74 × 18 = 562 + 740 = 1,302. What went wrong?
choices: 74 × 10 should be 74
74 × 8 should be 592: the regrouped 3 was never added
Nothing. 1,302 is right.
no: 74 × 10 = 740 is right: it needs the 0.
562 + 740 is 1,302. The adding is fine; the first row is wrong.
Check 74 × 8 again. Where did the regrouped 3 go?

items.q: Someone wrote: 76 × 38 = 608 + 2,280 = 2,848. What went wrong?
choices: 76 × 8 should be 568
76 × 30 should be 228
Nothing. 2,848 is right.
The rows were added wrong: 608 + 2,280 = 2,888
items.why: Both rows are right. Add again column by column: 608 + 2,280 = 2,888.
no: 76 × 8 = 608 is right.
76 × 30 needs the 0: 2,280 is right.
Add the rows again, one column at a time.

notes.do: He says WHICH row is wrong and WHY before choosing.
notes.say: These are your own two mistakes from the last few days. Find them like a teacher would.
notes.ask: Which mistake would the estimate catch?
notes.listen: Neither: both answers are close to the estimate. Only rechecking each step catches them.

slides.title: Three in a row
slides.text: Estimate, ones row, tens row, line up, add, compare. Paper first.

items.no: Ones row 68 × 7, tens row 68 × 20, then add.
Ones row 135 × 2, tens row 135 × 10, then add.
Ones row 216 × 4, tens row 216 × 10, then add.

notes.do: He works alone. If he misses one, stop and do one more on graph paper with you before moving on.
notes.say: These are the exact steps you'll use to check long division in a few minutes.
notes.ask: How do you know your answer is right?
notes.listen: It's close to my estimate AND I rechecked each row.

slides.title: Deja's problem
slides.text: Deja's class has 552 cans. There are 24 pantries. Each pantry should get the same number of cans.
prompts: Why does each pantry need the exact same number?
Is the answer closer to 2, 20 or 200? How do you know?
What could Deja do if some cans are left over?
starters: Each pantry needs the same number because …
I think it is close to … because …
If cans are left over, Deja could …

notes.do: 2 to 3 minutes. Write his guess for 552 ÷ 24 in the corner of the whiteboard. We come back to it.
notes.ask: How could multiplying help you guess? (24 × 10? 24 × 20?)
notes.listen: 24 × 20 = 480, so about 20. If he says 'about 20 something,' praise it: that is an estimate with multiplication, and it is exactly how we check today.

slides.title: Lesson 1 review and leftovers
slides.text: Paper first, then type. The first one is from Lesson 1.

items.q: Lesson 1 skill. Stack it: 24 × 23 = ____
items.why: 24 × 3 = 72 and 24 × 20 = 480. 72 + 480 = 552. That is Deja's number of cans!
items.no: Ones row: 24 × 3. Tens row: write the 0, then 24 × 2. Add.
Think: 7 times what is 56?

items.q: 47 ÷ 6 = ____ Type it like 5 R2.
items.no: How many 6s fit in 47 without going over?

items.q: Check it with multiplication: 6 × 7 + 5 = ____
items.why: 6 × 7 = 42, and 42 + 5 = 47. It matches, so 7 R5 is right.
items.no: Multiply first, then add the remainder.

notes.do: He answers out loud, writes on paper, then types. Circle the 552 on the whiteboard: it comes back in 10 minutes.
notes.say: Division and multiplication are a team. If 47 ÷ 6 = 7 R5, then 6 × 7 + 5 has to make 47.
notes.ask: Why did you not say 8 R-something for 47 ÷ 6?
notes.listen: 6 × 8 = 48 is more than 47. The quotient is the biggest number that fits without going over.

slides.title: Math words for today
slides.text: Tap each card to flip it. Read the word, the meaning and the example out loud.

words.meaning: The number being divided. It goes inside the long division box.
words.example: In 552 ÷ 24 = 23, the dividend is 552.

words.meaning: The number you are dividing BY. It goes outside the box.
words.example: In 552 ÷ 24 = 23, the divisor is 24.

words.meaning: The answer to a division problem.
words.example: In 552 ÷ 24 = 23, the quotient is 23.

words.meaning: What is left over when a number does not divide evenly. It must be smaller than the divisor.
words.example: 17 ÷ 5 = 3 R2. The remainder is 2.

words.meaning: The answer when you multiply a number by 1, 2, 3, and so on.
words.example: 24, 48, 72 and 96 are multiples of 24.

notes.do: He reads each card aloud, then covers it and says the meaning in his own words.
notes.say: You will type these from memory at the end of class and all week. Say each one out loud now.
notes.ask: Which number goes inside the box? Which goes outside? Which is the answer?
notes.listen: Dividend inside, divisor outside, quotient on top. Quotient is the word he has missed before: have him spell it out loud (q-u-o-t-i-e-n-t).

slides.title: Long division: 552 ÷ 4
slides.text: Deja first splits the 552 cans onto 4 carts. Build 552 with blocks: 5 hundreds, 5 tens, 2 ones. Share them into 4 equal groups.

steps.text: Divide. 5 hundreds ÷ 4 → 1 hundred in each group. Write the 1 above the 5.
Multiply. 1 × 4 = 4. Subtract. 5 − 4 = 1 hundred left. Trade it for 10 tens.
Bring down the 5: now there are 15 tens. 15 ÷ 4 → 3. 3 × 4 = 12. 15 − 12 = 3 tens left. Trade them for 30 ones.
Bring down the 2: now there are 32 ones. 32 ÷ 4 → 8. 8 × 4 = 32. 32 − 32 = 0.

slides.tip: Divide, Multiply, Subtract, Bring down. Then do it again. (Dad, Mom, Sister, Brother.)

notes.do: Hands-on: he builds 552 with base-ten blocks and shares them into 4 groups on the table. Each trade (1 hundred for 10 tens, 3 tens for 30 ones) is a 'bring down.' He writes each step on paper as he does it with the blocks.
notes.say: Every time you trade blocks, that is a bring down on paper. The paper and the blocks do the same thing.
notes.ask: Why did we trade the leftover hundred for tens? What does the 3 in 138 mean?
notes.listen: One hundred cannot be shared by 4 as a hundred, so it becomes 10 tens. The 3 means 3 tens (30 cans) in each group.

slides.title: Your turn: 552 ÷ 6
slides.text: Now the cans go onto 6 trucks. Write it on paper: Divide, Multiply, Subtract, Bring down.

items.q: 552 ÷ 6. The 5 is smaller than 6, so start with 55. How many 6s fit in 55?
items.why: 6 × 9 = 54, and 6 × 10 = 60 is too big. So 9.
items.no: Count by 6s: 48, 54, 60. Which is the biggest that fits?

items.q: Multiply 9 × 6 = 54. Subtract: 55 − 54 = ____
items.why: 55 − 54 = 1. 1 is smaller than 6, so we keep going.
items.no: Subtract the 54 from 55.

items.q: Bring down the 2 to make 12. How many 6s fit in 12?
items.why: 6 × 2 = 12. So 2, with 0 left.
items.no: Think 6 times what is 12?
Put the two quotient digits together: 9 and 2.
items.hint: The 9 goes over the second 5; the 2 goes over the 2.

notes.do: He talks through each step out loud while he writes. You only ask questions.
notes.ask: Where does the 9 go on top? Why not over the first 5?
notes.listen: 6 does not fit into 5, so the first digit goes over the second 5 (the tens place). The answer has 2 digits, not 3.

slides.title: Remainders, and checking with multiplication
slides.text: 5 more cans arrive. Now it is 557 ÷ 6.

steps.text: Same steps: 55 ÷ 6 → 9, 55 − 54 = 1. Bring down the 7 to make 17.
17 ÷ 6 → 2. 2 × 6 = 12. 17 − 12 = 5. There is nothing left to bring down.
The 5 is the remainder: 557 ÷ 6 = 92 R5. The remainder must be smaller than the divisor (5 is less than 6).
Check with multiplication: divisor × quotient + remainder = dividend. 6 × 92 + 5 = 552 + 5 = 557. ✅

slides.tip: Check every answer: multiply the quotient by the divisor, then add the remainder. You should get the dividend back.

notes.do: He writes the check under his work every time from now on: 6 × 92 + 5 = 557.
notes.say: The check is your Lesson 1 skill doing a job. If the check does not give you the dividend, there is a mistake.
notes.ask: What if your remainder came out as 8? What would that tell you?
notes.listen: 8 is bigger than 6, so another 6 fits. The quotient digit is too small.

slides.title: Remainders and the check
slides.text: Paper first. Write the check under every problem.

items.q: 389 ÷ 4 = ____ Type it like 5 R2.
items.no: Start with 38, since 4 does not fit into 3.

items.q: Check your answer: 4 × 97 + 1 = ____
items.why: 4 × 97 = 388, and 388 + 1 = 389. It matches the dividend. ✅
items.no: Multiply 97 × 4 first. Then add 1.
Start with 73, since 8 does not fit into 7.

notes.do: Hands off. He writes the work and the check on paper before he types.
notes.ask: How did your check prove 91 R3?
notes.listen: 8 × 91 = 728, and 728 + 3 = 731. Watch for him typing 91.3 or 913: the answer format is 91 R3.

slides.title: Two-digit divisors: 552 ÷ 24
slides.text: Back to Deja's real problem. Step 0: make a multiples list for 24. It turns guessing into looking.

steps.text: Estimate. 24 × 20 = 480 and 24 × 30 = 720. So 552 ÷ 24 is between 20 and 30.
Divide. 24 does not fit into 5. Look at 55. The list says 48 fits and 72 is too big, so → 2.
Multiply 2 × 24 = 48. Subtract 55 − 48 = 7. Bring down the 2 to make 72.
Check: 24 × 23 = 552. You already did that in the warm-up! ✅ Each pantry gets 23 cans. Is 23 between 20 and 30? Yes.

slides.tip: With a 2-digit divisor, write the multiples list first. Then each step is just looking it up.

notes.do: He builds the multiples list on an index card by adding 24 each time, then checks 24 × 5 = 120 with multiplication. He keeps the card for the rest of the math.
notes.say: Same four steps as before. The only new thing is the list. Look back at your guess from 9:30.
notes.ask: Why is 2 the first quotient digit and not 3?
notes.listen: 24 × 3 = 72 is more than 55. The biggest multiple that fits under 55 is 48.

slides.title: Reading words for today
slides.text: Tap each card. Read the word, the meaning and the example out loud.

words.meaning: The way a person sees or feels about something, based on what matters most to them.
words.example: Malia's viewpoint is that a hamster would teach responsibility.

words.meaning: To look at how two or more things are the SAME.
words.example: When I compare Malia and Theo, I see they both care about the class.

words.meaning: To look at how two or more things are DIFFERENT.
words.example: When I contrast them, Malia wants a hamster and Theo wants a fish tank.

words.meaning: The thinking or logic behind why someone believes something.
words.example: Theo's reasoning: a hamster needs care every day, even on breaks.

words.meaning: Specific facts or details that support a viewpoint.
words.example: "A few kids in our class are allergic to fur" is evidence.

words.meaning: Meant to convince the reader to agree.
words.example: Malia's piece is persuasive writing: she wants your vote.

words.meaning: A plan where each side gives up a little so both can agree.
words.example: A fish tank is a compromise: a class pet with no fur.

notes.do: He reads each card aloud and covers it. Spend extra time on evidence and compromise: he has had trouble typing those from memory.
notes.say: Now we switch to reading. Two kids, one class vote, and two very different viewpoints.
notes.ask: What is the difference between compare and contrast?
notes.listen: Compare = how they are the same. Contrast = how they are different.

slides.title: Malia's case
slides.text: Mrs. Chen's class is voting on whether to get a class hamster. Read Malia's piece out loud.

visual.text:
Malia writes (for the hamster):
“A class hamster would teach us real responsibility. We'd take turns feeding it, cleaning its cage, and learning about how animals live. My cousin's class had a guinea pig, and everyone learned so much about caring for something besides themselves. It made the whole class feel closer, too.”

items.q: What does Malia care about MOST in her piece?
choices: How cute hamsters are
Learning responsibility and bringing the class closer
Getting out of homework
Winning the vote no matter what
items.why: She says a hamster 'would teach us real responsibility' and 'made the whole class feel closer.'
no: She never says hamsters are cute. Look for what she says a pet would TEACH.
Homework is not in her piece.
She gives reasons. She does not say winning is what matters.

items.q: Malia's cousin's class had a pet. What kind of animal was it? Type it.
items.why: Malia writes: 'My cousin's class had a guinea pig.'
items.no: Look at the sentence about her cousin.
items.hint: It is two words. It is not a hamster.

items.q: Malia says a class hamster would teach real ________. Type the word.
items.why: Her first sentence: 'A class hamster would teach us real responsibility.'
items.no: Look at her first sentence.

notes.do: He reads aloud and highlights Malia's reasons in color 1 on paper (or points to them on screen).
notes.ask: Which sentence is her opinion? Which sentence is a real example?
notes.listen: Opinion: a hamster would teach responsibility. Real example: her cousin's class had a guinea pig and everyone learned.

slides.title: Theo's case
slides.text: Now read Theo's piece out loud.

visual.text:
Theo writes (against the hamster):
“I love animals, but a classroom isn't the best place for one. Someone has to remember to feed it every single day, including weekends and school breaks. A few kids in our class are allergic to fur, too. I think we should get a class fish tank instead. It's calming, and nobody's allergic to fish.”

items.q: Theo says a few kids in the class are allergic to ____. Type the word.
items.why: Theo writes: 'A few kids in our class are allergic to fur.'
items.no: Look for the word allergic.

items.q: Theo starts with “I love animals, but…” What does that tell you about his viewpoint?
choices: He dislikes all animals
He has never seen a hamster
He likes animals, but thinks a classroom is not the best place for one
He agrees with Malia completely
items.why: He says he loves animals. The word but shows his worry is about the classroom, not about animals.
no: He says 'I love animals,' so he does not dislike them.
Nothing in his piece says that.
He suggests a fish tank instead, so he does not agree completely.

items.q: What does Theo want the class to get instead of a hamster? Type it.
items.why: Theo writes: 'I think we should get a class fish tank instead.'
items.no: Look at his last two sentences.
items.hint: It is calming, and nobody is allergic to it.

notes.do: He highlights Theo's reasons in color 2.
notes.ask: Is Theo against ALL class pets? How do you know?
notes.listen: No. He wants a fish tank. He is against a hamster because of daily care and fur allergies.

slides.title: Compare and contrast
slides.text: Strong readers do not just pick a side. They notice what each person cares about most.

visual.text: compare = SAME · contrast = DIFFERENT

steps.text: Compare (same): Both care about the class. Both like animals. Both actually want some kind of class pet.
Contrast (different): Malia wants a hamster; Theo wants a fish tank.
Contrast (different): Malia focuses on what the class would learn. Theo focuses on practical problems: feeding it every day, even on breaks, and fur allergies.
Why? They weigh different things as most important. That is what makes a viewpoint.

slides.tip: Use clue words. Same: both, also, alike. Different: but, while, instead.

notes.do: Hands-on: draw a T-chart on the whiteboard (Same | Different). He fills it from his two highlight colors BEFORE you click the steps. Then compare his chart to the steps.
notes.say: Compare is same. Contrast is different. Say a sentence with 'both' and a sentence with 'while.'
notes.ask: Give me one sentence that compares them and one that contrasts them.
notes.listen: 'Both Malia and Theo care about the class.' 'Malia focuses on learning, while Theo focuses on daily care.'

visual.text:
Malia writes (for the hamster):
“A class hamster would teach us real responsibility. We'd take turns feeding it, cleaning its cage, and learning about how animals live. My cousin's class had a guinea pig, and everyone learned so much about caring for something besides themselves. It made the whole class feel closer, too.”

Theo writes (against the hamster):
“I love animals, but a classroom isn't the best place for one. Someone has to remember to feed it every single day, including weekends and school breaks. A few kids in our class are allergic to fur, too. I think we should get a class fish tank instead. It's calming, and nobody's allergic to fish.”

items.q: Which is the STRONGEST evidence in Theo's piece?
choices: Fish are prettier than hamsters
Theo just does not feel like it
A few kids in the class are allergic to fur
Theo's cousin has a pet
items.why: It is a real fact that would affect students in the class. That makes it strong evidence.
no: Theo never says that. It would only be a feeling anyway.
That is not in his piece, and a feeling is weak evidence.
That is Malia's cousin, and Theo never mentions a cousin.

items.q: Why is Theo's fish tank idea a compromise?
choices: It gives the class a pet but avoids the fur and daily-feeding problems
It means the class gets no pet at all
It means Malia wins the vote
Fish tanks are required by the school
items.why: Each side gets something: the class still has a pet (Malia's side), with no fur allergy problem (Theo's side).
no: A fish tank IS a class pet.
Malia wanted a hamster, not a fish tank.
Nothing in the text says that.

items.q: Compare them: Malia and Theo BOTH want the class to have some kind of class ________. Type the word.
items.why: Malia wants a hamster and Theo wants a fish tank, so both want a class pet.
items.no: What do a hamster and a fish tank have in common here?
items.hint: Malia wants a hamster. Theo wants fish.

notes.do: He reads both pieces again (scroll) and points to the exact sentence for each answer.
notes.ask: Which is stronger evidence: 'my cousin's class loved it' or 'a few kids are allergic'? Why?
notes.listen: Both are real details, but the allergy fact is about THIS class and affects real students, so most kids will weigh it more.

slides.title: How would you vote?
slides.text: Use evidence from BOTH pieces.
prompts: How would you vote: hamster, fish tank, or no pet? Give one piece of evidence from the text.
What is the strongest point from the side you did NOT pick?
Can you think of a different compromise?
starters: I would vote for … because the text says …
The strongest point on the other side is …

notes.do: Tap the gold star when he quotes the text. Push for exact words from the passage, not just 'because I like fish.'
notes.ask: Why is it useful to read BOTH pieces before you vote?
notes.listen: Each writer points out things the other one does not. A good decision weighs the benefits AND the problems.

slides.title: Two big skills
slides.text: You split big numbers fairly, and you weighed two viewpoints fairly.

steps.text: Long division: Divide, Multiply, Subtract, Bring down. Repeat.
Two-digit divisor? Make a multiples list first.
Check: divisor × quotient + remainder = dividend. The remainder must be smaller than the divisor.
Read the question again: round up, drop the remainder, or the remainder is the answer.
Reading: compare (same), contrast (different), and weigh the evidence from BOTH sides.

slides.tip: Slow and right beats fast and wrong. Write the check, then type carefully.

notes.do: Open the course page together and read this week's task list, one day at a time.
notes.say: Tonight: the after-class lesson and Show What You Know. A little each day after that. Tuesday: Pathways Week 7 Math.
notes.ask: Say the four division steps and the check without looking.
notes.listen: Divide, multiply, subtract, bring down; then divisor × quotient + remainder. If he skips the check, remind him: that is where the points are saved.

slides.title: Deja's Food Drive: On Your Own
slides.text: In class you learned long division and how to compare two viewpoints. Now you do it on your own. Keep paper and a pencil next to you. Work every division problem on paper and write the check.

slides.title: Explain it out loud
slides.text: Say these to a grown-up, or say them out loud to yourself.
prompts: What are the four steps of long division? What do you do after the last step?
Deja packs 170 cans in boxes of 24: 170 ÷ 24 = 7 R2. Why can a remainder mean round up one time and drop it another time?
What is the difference between compare and contrast? Use Malia and Theo.
starters: It depends on the question, because …

slides.title: Divide, Multiply, Subtract, Bring down, Check
slides.tip: Check: 24 × 23 + 17 = 552 + 17 = 569. ✅ The remainder 17 is smaller than 24.

slides.title: One-digit divisors
slides.text: Paper first. Write the check under each one.

items.no: Start with 8. Divide, multiply, subtract, bring down.

items.q: 925 ÷ 4 = ____ Type it like 5 R2.
items.no: 9 ÷ 4 → 2, 1 left. Bring down the 2.
Multiply 231 × 4 first, then add the remainder.

slides.title: Two-digit divisors
slides.text: Make the multiples list first.

items.q: Multiples of 28: 28, 56, 84, ____
items.no: Add 28 to 84.
How many 28s fit in 67? Use your list.

slides.text: Divide, then read the question again.

teacher.objective: Review first (20 min): Ethan fixes the Lesson 1 steps he has not mastered (tens row with the 0, lining up columns on graph paper, adding the partial products, estimating with the right number of zeros, checking his own work). Then Lesson 2 math (18 min): long division with 1-digit divisors, remainders, and the check divisor × quotient + remainder = dividend, previewing 2-digit divisors if time allows. Reading (18 min): compare and contrast two viewpoints in The Class Pet Vote using evidence from the text. After class he retakes Lesson 1 on his own (85 needed) before the Lesson 2 after-class lesson opens.
materials: The class lesson on a laptop or tablet (teacher code 9110)
Graph Paper Practice (graph-paper-01.pdf), or graph paper / lined paper turned sideways
Base-ten blocks: for 36 × 40, and for 552 ÷ 4 (5 flats, 15 rods, 32 units)
Whiteboard and two marker colors; two highlighters (one for Malia, one for Theo)
Pencil and paper; Lesson 2 Packet (2 pages), printed: page 1 Saturday, page 2 Sunday

plan.do: Class slide 1. Tell him why we review first. Write the three steps on the whiteboard: estimate · ones row + tens row · line up and add.
Slides 2–3. Blocks for 36 × 40; he says “forty” and writes the 0 first. 56 × 40, 47 × 30, the tens row of 68 × 27.
Slide 4. 68 × 27 on graph paper, one digit per square, regroup marks above.
Slide 6. His own mistakes: 74 × 18 and 76 × 38. He names the row and the reason.

plan.block: 9:47 · Three in a row (on his own)
plan.do: Slide 7. 68 × 27, 135 × 12, 216 × 14. A miss means one more on graph paper with you.
Slides 8–9. He guesses 552 ÷ 24. 24 × 23 = 552 (multiplication he just fixed), 56 ÷ 7, 47 ÷ 6 = 7 R5 and its check.
Slide 10. Dividend, divisor, quotient, remainder, multiple.
Slide 11. Base-ten blocks shared into 4 groups; each trade is a bring down. Answer 138, checked with 138 × 4.
Slide 12. He talks through each step. Answer 92.
Slides 13–14. 557 ÷ 6 = 92 R5. He writes divisor × quotient + remainder under every problem, on graph paper.
Slide 15 (552 ÷ 24 = 23 with a multiples list). 569 ÷ 24, what a remainder means in a story, and the division checker are in his after-class lesson.
Slide 16. Viewpoint, compare, contrast, reasoning, evidence, persuasive, compromise.
Slides 17–18. He reads aloud and highlights each writer's reasons in a different color.
Slides 19–20. Whiteboard T-chart (Same | Different) from his highlights, then the strongest evidence and the compromise.
Slide 21. He votes and gives one piece of evidence in the text's exact words.

Slide 22, then show the course card: first the Retake Lesson 1 button (on his own, after class), then the After-class lesson, which opens when he scores 85. Read the task list together, including the retake rule.

watch: Tens row: he must say the tens digit as tens (“forty”) and write the 0 first. 56 × 40 = 324 was his mistake: he treated 40 as 4.
Columns: one digit per square on graph paper; regrouped 1s written above the column. Most of his wrong answers (1,786 for 1,836; 2,848 for 2,888; 1,350 for 1,620) came from adding the rows.
Estimate: 70 × 20 = 1,400, not 14,000. He writes the estimate in a box before every problem.
Rushing on retakes: his scores have dropped on repeat tries (Pathways Week 6 Math 80, 63, 55; Week 3 Reading 75, 25). Retakes come after the problems are worked on paper, one retake a day.

Where the first digit goes: when the divisor does not fit into the first digit (552 ÷ 6), the first quotient digit goes over the SECOND digit. If he writes 0 or a digit over the 5, ask: how many 6s fit in 5?
Bring down every digit: his answer must use every digit of the dividend. 552 ÷ 6 = 9 R1 means he stopped early. The check catches it: 6 × 9 + 1 = 55, not 552.
Remainder size: the remainder must be smaller than the divisor. 12 R11 for 95 ÷ 7, or 28 R24 for 696 ÷ 24, pass the multiplication check, so he also needs this rule.

Multiples list for 2-digit divisors: he writes it on the side BEFORE dividing, by adding the divisor each time, and checks the 5th multiple with multiplication. Guessing without the list leads to erasing.
The check: divisor × quotient + remainder = dividend, written under every problem. This is his Lesson 1 multiplication doing a job; watch his regrouping in the multiplication too.

Typing remainders: the answer format is 92 R5 (spaces and lower case are fine). Watch for 92.5 or 925. He has lost points on typed answers that were right on paper, so he checks the typed answer against his paper before pressing Check.

Remainder in a story: he rereads the question after dividing. Round up when everything needs a place (vans, buses, boxes for ALL), drop it when only full groups count, and give the remainder when the question asks what is left. Typing 7 R2 for a number of boxes is the mistake to catch.
Reading: he reads fast and accurately, so push for exact words from the text as proof. 'Because I think so' is not evidence. Compare uses both/also; contrast uses but/while/instead.
